queries.hook: I can't stop overthinking. Inside, my mind won't settle, and I don't know how to carry it.
queries.diagnose: The untrained mind runs like the wind, replaying and imagining; left to itself it becomes its own enemy.
queries.steady: The mind can be trained slowly, by practice and letting go; each time it wanders, it can be gently brought back.
queries.act: Bring the mind back each time it wanders, with practice and letting go; make the mind your friend through steady practice.

hook.speaker: Krishna
hook.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
hook.sanskrit: यतो यतो निश्चरति मनश्चञ्चलमस्थिरम् । ततस्ततो नियम्यैतदात्मन्येव वशं नयेत् ॥
hook.line: Wherever the restless mind wanders, gently bring it back. Again and again.
hook.translation: Wherever the restless, unsteady mind wanders, from there one should draw it back and bring it under the control of the self.
hook.why: Moderation and gentle return, again and again, settle the mind.

prasang.title: Meditation in detail
prasang.summary: Krishna describes meditation: moderation in food and sleep, the mind like a lamp in a windless place, bringing the wandering mind back, and feeling others' joy and pain as one's own.
prasang.lesson: Moderation and gentle return, again and again, settle the mind.

alternates.speaker: Arjuna
alternates.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
alternates.sanskrit: चञ्चलं हि मनः कृष्ण प्रमाथि बलवद्दृढम् । तस्याहं निग्रहं मन्ये वायोरिव सुदुष्करम् ॥
alternates.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
alternates.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.
alternates.why: The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.

prasang.title: Mastering the mind
prasang.summary: Arjuna says the mind is restless, stormy and stubborn. Krishna agrees, and says practice and letting go can train it.
prasang.lesson: The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.

alternates.speaker: Krishna
alternates.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how to act without being chained to results.
alternates.sanskrit: व्यवसायात्मिका बुद्धिरेकेह कुरुनन्दन । बहुशाखा ह्यनन्ताश्च बुद्धयोऽव्यवसायिनाम् ॥
alternates.line: A decided mind is single and focused. An undecided mind splits into endless branches.
alternates.translation: Here, Arjuna, the resolute mind is one-pointed. But the thoughts of the irresolute are many-branched and endless.
alternates.why: Do the work fully; let go of owning the result.

prasang.title: The yoga of action
prasang.summary: Krishna teaches the yoga of action: work wholeheartedly, give up clinging to outcomes, stay even in success and failure, and keep a single steady purpose.
prasang.lesson: Do the work fully; let go of owning the result.

prasang.title: Meditation in detail
prasang.summary: Krishna describes meditation: moderation in food and sleep, the mind like a lamp in a windless place, bringing the wandering mind back, and feeling others' joy and pain as one's own.
prasang.lesson: Moderation and gentle return, again and again, settle the mind.

verse.meaning: Krishna is teaching Arjuna how to sit still in meditation. He says the mind wanders. It is restless and unsteady. When it wanders, you could gently pull it back. You bring it back to yourself. You do this again and again.
verse.for_you: You are trying to build something and care for your parents, but your mind is running in circles. It is not your fault. It just has no habit of stopping.
verse.try_today: Notice when your mind has wandered and gently bring it back to one thing.
verse.scene_line: You are sitting in your own quiet place, and your mind is like a horse that keeps breaking its reins.
asks: How do I know when my mind has wandered too far?
What does it mean to bring the mind back to myself?

verse.speaker: Rama
verse.setting: Rama, near the end of his lament, says where the real enemy lives.
verse.sanskrit: शत्रवश्चेन्द्रियाण्येव सत्यं यातमसत्यताम् । प्रहरत्यात्मनैवात्मा मनसैव मनो रिपुः ॥
verse.line: No one hurts us like we hurt ourselves. The mind becomes the mind's own enemy.
verse.translation: Our own senses are the enemies; truth itself has turned untrue; the self strikes the self, and the mind is the mind's own enemy.
verse.why: Naming honestly what feels empty is the first step; Rama's lament is a question, not the answer.
verse.misuse: Not a reason to blame yourself. Vasishtha's answer is that the same mind can lift itself.

prasang.title: Rama's lament: what is the point of all this?
prasang.summary: Asked to speak, Rama pours out what he has seen: wealth hardens people, life drips away like water off a leaf, ego and craving run us, the mind never fills, childhood, youth and old age each bring their own suffering, and time eats everything. He ends by saying only the company of good people gives him hope.
prasang.story_hook: In front of the whole court, the young prince stood up and said what everyone feels and nobody says.
prasang.lesson: Naming honestly what feels empty is the first step; Rama's lament is a question, not the answer.

verse.meaning: Rama is in the middle of a deep lament. They have just told the sages that wealth hardens people, life slips away, and the mind never fills. In that moment of despair, they say that our own senses are the enemies, the self strikes the self, and the mind becomes the mind's own enemy. The verse names the pattern honestly: the restlessness is not an outside force. It is the mind turning on itself. This is not the final answer, but it is the honest first step of seeing the pattern clearly.
verse.for_you: Your mind has been running its own race all day, and now you are seeing that the track is inside your own head. It is not a flaw, just a habit that was never taught to stop.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment when your mind attacks itself, and let it pass.
verse.scene_line: You are in your own lament, seeing the mind turn on itself.
asks: What part of my mind is my own enemy?
How do I stop the self from striking the self?
Is this restlessness something I can name without blame?

verse.speaker: Ribhu
verse.sanskrit: यानि दुःखानि या तृष्णा दुःसहा ये दुराधयः । शान्तचेतःसु तत्सर्वं तमोऽर्केष्विव नश्यति ॥
verse.line: Sorrow, craving and unbearable anxiety all vanish in a calm mind, like darkness before the sun.
verse.translation: Whatever sorrows, whatever craving, whatever unbearable anxieties there are, all of them vanish in calm minds, as darkness vanishes before the sun.
verse.why: Start with calm or contentment, and the rest follows.

prasang.title: Ribhu on calm and contentment
prasang.summary: Ribhu answers Nidagha: freedom has four gatekeepers (calm, inquiry, contentment and good company), and winning one brings the rest. In a calm mind sorrow and anxiety vanish; restlessness is simply the mind's nature, and only your own mind can lift you out.
prasang.lesson: Start with calm or contentment, and the rest follows.

verse.for_you: You are not the mind; thoughts come and go before the silent witness that watches them and is never disturbed.
verse.scene_line: You are sitting in the quiet before the sun, watching the darkness lift.
asks: How do I let the mind rest without forcing it?

verse.speaker: Bhushunda
verse.setting: Bhushunda, the ancient crow who has watched the ages pass, tells Vasishtha why he lives long and well.
verse.sanskrit: न भूतं न भविष्यं च चिन्तयामि कदाचन । दृष्टिमालम्ब्य तिष्ठामि वर्तमानामिहात्मना ॥
verse.line: I don't brood over the past or the future. I keep my attention on now.
verse.translation: I never brood over the past or the future. I hold my attention on the present, here, with myself.
verse.why: A long, steady life comes from a mind that stays in the present, wants little and stays kind.

prasang.title: Bhushunda, the crow who outlived the ages
prasang.summary: Vasishtha travels to a wish-fulfilling tree on Mount Meru to meet Bhushunda, a crow who has watched world-ages come and go. Asked how he has lived so long, untroubled, Bhushunda lists his habits: he doesn't brood on the past or future, doesn't fret about what he'll get next, doesn't grow arrogant from knowing, and shares in others' joys and sorrows.
prasang.story_hook: High on a mountain lived a crow who had watched whole ages of the world rise and fall.
prasang.lesson: A long, steady life comes from a mind that stays in the present, wants little and stays kind.

verse.meaning: Bhushunda, the ancient crow who has watched the ages pass, tells Vasishtha why he lives long and well. He says he never broods over the past or the future. He holds his attention on the present, here, with himself. A long and steady life comes from a mind that stays in the now, wants little, and stays kind.
verse.for_you: It is not a moral failing. It is a habit you can loosen. The present is not a place you reach.
verse.try_today: Notice one thing you are doing right now, and let it have your full attention for ten seconds.
verse.scene_line: You are on a branch that has lasted through many ages.
asks: How do I stop the mind from running ahead?

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Arjuna asks which devotee is best; Krishna offers a ladder of practices.
verse.line: Practice is good, understanding better, meditation better still. But letting go of results brings peace at once.
verse.translation: Knowledge is better than mere practice; meditation is better than knowledge; giving up the fruit of action is better than meditation. From that renunciation, peace follows immediately.
verse.why: If the ideal is too hard, take the next step down, and keep going.
verse.misuse: Not 'stop caring how things turn out'. Peace comes from releasing the grip, not from indifference.

prasang.title: Form or formless: which devotee is best, and the ways to reach him
prasang.summary: Krishna says devotion to a personal form is easier, then offers a ladder: fix your mind; if not, practise; if not, work for me; if not, let go of results. Letting go brings peace at once.
prasang.lesson: If the ideal is too hard, take the next step down, and keep going.

verse.meaning: Arjuna asks which kind of devotee is best. Krishna answers with a ladder of practices. Fix your mind on me, he says. If that is too hard, practise. If that is too hard, work for me. If that is too hard, let go of results. Letting go of results brings peace at once. The verse proposes that if the highest ideal feels out of reach, you can step down to the next rung. You do not have to do it all at once.
verse.for_you: You are trying to hold the future together with your own hands, and it is exhausting. The verse does not ask you to stop caring. It asks you to loosen the grip. You are building your own thing, studying, and caring for your parents. You can do all of that.
verse.try_today: When you notice your mind spinning, name one thing you are trying to control.
verse.scene_line: You are at the bottom of the ladder, and the next step down is relief.
asks: How do I let go of results without giving up on my work?
Can I find peace in the middle of building something?

verse.speaker: Vasishtha
verse.setting: Vasishtha on effort and grace, after Prahlada's story.
verse.sanskrit: नित्याभ्यासविवेकाभ्यां चित्तमाशु प्रसीदति । आम्र एव दशामेति साहकारीं शनैः शनैः ॥
verse.line: Daily practice and clear thinking make the mind clear, slowly, the way a mango ripens.
verse.translation: Through daily practice and discernment the mind soon becomes clear, just as a mango slowly ripens into its sweetness.
verse.why: Grace and effort work together; keep practising daily, and let the mind ripen slowly.

prasang.title: Prahlada: effort and grace are not rivals
prasang.summary: After telling how Prahlada awakened, Vasishtha faces Rama's challenge: if everything comes by effort, wasn't Prahlada saved by Vishnu's grace? Vasishtha answers that Prahlada earned it himself, that the Self and Vishnu are not two, and that sometimes we wake by our own effort and sometimes by grace reached through devotion. Steady daily practice ripens the mind like a mango.
prasang.lesson: Grace and effort work together; keep practising daily, and let the mind ripen slowly.

verse.meaning: Vasishtha is speaking to Rama, who has been listening to the story of Prahlada. Rama wonders if Prahlada was saved by his own effort or by Vishnu's grace. Vasishtha replies that Prahlada earned his awakening through steady practice, just as a mango slowly ripens into sweetness. The verse says that daily practice and clear thinking make the mind clear slowly. It means you could keep practising every day, and let the mind ripen in its own time. You do not force the fruit, you tend the tree and trust the season.
verse.for_you: Bring the mind back each time it wanders, with practice and letting go; make the mind your friend through steady practice.
verse.try_today: Do one small practice without checking the result.
verse.scene_line: You are standing at the tree, waiting for the mango to ripen.
asks: How do I practice without checking the result?
How do I stop shaking the tree?

story.title: King Janaka overhears the sages and keeps ruling, with a free mind
story.story_hook: One spring morning, a king out for a walk overheard a song that he could not stop thinking about.
story.summary: Walking in his spring garden, King Janaka overhears hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. When his doorkeeper calls him to the day's work, he decides not to run away: he gets up and does his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutches.
story.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

anchor.speaker: Janaka
anchor.setting: King Janaka, alone on his palace roof after overhearing wandering sages, rethinks his life.
anchor.sanskrit: संपदश्च विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेच्चित्तेन संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा हन्त मन्ये महापदः ॥ आपदोऽपि विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेन्मनसि संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा मन्ये मनसि संपदः ॥
anchor.line: Good fortune the mind clutches becomes trouble. Trouble the mind accepts becomes a kind of fortune.
anchor.translation: All those dazzling fortunes, if the mind clings to them, are really great calamities in grand disguise. And all those varied misfortunes, if the mind accepts them, are really fortunes.
anchor.why: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.
anchor.misuse: Accepting a hardship doesn't mean not fixing what can be fixed.

story.for_you: Janaka stood on his roof and saw that his kingdom was still there, his duties were still there. Your work and your care for your parents are still there too. They do not need your mind to clutch them.
